content: Your physician has prescribed Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) for you. This treatment involves delivering nutrients directly into your bloodstream through a needle or catheter inserted into a vein. The infusion typically lasts 10-12 hours and is administered either daily or five times a week. TPN is specifically designed for individuals who are unable to obtain adequate nutrition through oral intake or for whom eating is contraindicated. The TPN solution may contain a combination of sugars and carbohydrates (to provide energy), proteins (to support muscle maintenance and repair), lipids (fats), electrolytes, and trace elements. The exact composition of your TPN solution will depend on your specific medical condition and nutritional needs. Although TPN often includes lipids, it will not cause weight gain or make you fat. Calories, proteins, and fats are essential components of a healthy diet, and your body requires these nutrients to function properly. Electrolytes, such as sodium, potassium, chloride, phosphate, calcium, and magnesium, are critical for maintaining the proper function of your organs, including your heart, muscles, and nerves. They also help prevent dehydration. Trace elements, including zinc, copper, manganese, and chromium, are also included in the solution to support various physiological processes. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of your TPN therapy and check for potential side effects through regular laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is essential to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your TPN treatment will depend on how well your body responds to the therapy. Precautions Before Starting TPN Before beginning TPN, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have any known allergies to medications. Notify your doctor if you have a history of diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, lung disease, or Addison's disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss the potential risks and benefits of TPN with your doctor. If you continue TPN during pregnancy or breastfeeding, your doctor may adjust the composition of your solution to meet your specific needs. Administering TPN Before administering your TPN solution, carefully inspect it. The solution should be clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it. Do not use the solution if it appears discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is damaged. If you encounter any issues with the solution, use a new one and show the damaged product to your healthcare provider. It is crucial to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when administering TPN. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your provider. Side Effects of TPN Minor Side Effects TPN may cause some minor side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they persist or worsen: Mouth sores Poor night vision Changes in your skin Severe Side Effects Seek immediate medical attention if you experience any of the following severe side effects: Fever or chills Abdominal pain Difficulty breathing Rapid weight gain or loss Increased urination Nausea or vomiting Confusion or memory problems Muscle weakness, twitching, or cramps Swelling in the hands, feet, or legs Excessive thirst Fatigue Irregular heartbeat Tingling sensations in the hands or feet Overactive reflexes Seizures or convulsions If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Storing TPN Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days' worth of TPN at a time. Store the TPN solution in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator 4-6 hours in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional TPN in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day for the following day's use. Do not refreeze TPN once it has been thawed. Keep all supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will provide instructions on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. Emergency and Overdose In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Signs of Infection If you are receiving TPN through a vein or under the skin, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter insertion site: Tenderness Warmth Irritation Drainage Redness Swelling Pain Other Names for TPN Total Parenteral Nutrition is also commonly referred to as TPN.
